formulas.name: Debt raised
formulas.note: Pennard: 5.0× on £50m = £250m, blending to 6 % cash interest. Lenders set the turns; the sponsor takes what is offered.

formulas.name: Sponsor equity (the plug)
formulas.note: Uses run £400m EV + £10m fees = £410m; less £250m of debt leaves a £160m cheque — 39 % of the deal, and not £150m, because the fees are a use.

formulas.name: Free cash flow
formulas.note: Pennard year 1: 52.5 − 15.0 − 6.9 − 10 = £20.6m, every pound of it swept against the debt. When capex equals D&A, FCF equals net income.

formulas.name: Exit equity
formulas.note: 8.0× on £63.8m = £510.4m, less the £115.7m still owed = £394.7m. Remaining debt — never the debt you started with.

formulas.name: Money multiple and IRR
formulas.note: £394.7m on £160m is 2.47×; over five years that is 2.47^{0.2} − 1 ≈ 19.8 %. MoM ignores time; IRR punishes a slow deal.

formulas.name: Rule of 72
formulas.note: At 20 % money doubles in about 3.6 years — the sanity check on any anchor you quote.

canonical.a: A sponsor buys a company using mostly debt — typically half to two-thirds of the price — and a minority equity cheque. The debt is raised against the target's cash flows and sits on its balance sheet; the company repays it from free cash flow over a four-to-six-year hold. At exit the business is sold, ideally at the same or better multiple, and because the cheque was small the return on it is magnified.

canonical.q: What makes a good LBO candidate?
canonical.a: Stable, predictable cash flows to service the debt; low capital requirements so cash converts; scope to take cost out; a capable management team; assets or contracts a lender can underwrite; and an entry price that is not already full. Cyclical earnings, heavy capex and regulatory exposure all cap the leverage a deal can carry.

Uses are what the money buys: the purchase price, any existing debt refinanced at close, and fees. Sources are where it comes from: senior debt sized by the lenders in turns of EBITDA, perhaps a junior layer, and the sponsor's equity — the plug that makes the sides balance. On Pennard, £410m of uses is funded £250m debt and £160m equity, about 60/40.

canonical.q: How does the sponsor make money?
canonical.a: Three levers. EBITDA growth: the business is worth more at exit. Deleveraging: free cash flow repays debt, so more of the exit value belongs to the equity. Multiple expansion: selling on a better multiple than you paid — which sponsors do not underwrite. Leverage amplifies whatever the levers deliver. On Pennard, growth adds about £110m and paydown about £134m; the multiple adds nothing, and £160m becomes roughly £395m.

Sources and uses first: 8× on £50m is £400m, plus £10m of fees; five turns of debt is £250m, so the cheque is £160m. Then cash: EBITDA less interest, tax and capex runs roughly £20m rising to £34m, all of it repaying debt — call it £135m over the hold. Exit at 8× on £64m is about £510m; take off the £115m still owed and the equity is £395m. That is 2.5× on £160m — around 20 %.

traps: Saying the sponsor repays the debt. The company does, from its own free cash flow — which is why cash generation beats growth as the screening question.
Treating leverage as a value creator. It concentrates the value on a smaller cheque and adds interest and risk; the value itself comes from the three levers.
Computing equity as 100 % minus the leverage. Equity is the plug on the uses side — fees and refinanced debt both enlarge the cheque.
Subtracting entry debt at exit. The business has been repaying it for five years; use the remaining balance, and the difference is exactly the paydown.
Building a full debt schedule in a paper LBO. Round aggressively and narrate the structure — precision is not what is being tested.
one_liners: Debt shrinks the cheque; cash flow shrinks the debt; the exit pays the equity.
you_may_hear: Cash sweeps and minimum-cash assumptions in the debt schedule.
PIK toggles — interest accrued onto the principal instead of paid in cash.
Maintenance vs incurrence covenants, and covenant-lite loans.
Dividend recapitalisations — re-levering mid-hold to return cash early.
